claims.claim: TBOA increased the peak spiking probability over 250% following climbing fiber stimulation.
claims.source: TBOA increased the peak spiking probability over 250% as well as increased the time window of spiking, consistent with spillover signaling (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: TBOA increased the time window of spiking following climbing fiber stimulation.
claims.source: TBOA increased the peak spiking probability over 250% as well as increased the time window of spiking, consistent with spillover signaling (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: TBOA reduced Golgi cell action potential probability to approximately 70% of baseline ~200 ms after climbing fiber stimulation.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, TBOA subsequently reduced GoC AP probability to approximately 70% of baseline (Figure 4B, ~200 ms after CF stimulation, arrow).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber stimulation can regulate Golgi cell spiking in a biphasic manner with both the increase and decrease in excitability regulated by glutamate transporters.
claims.source: This suggests that CF stimulation can regulate GoC spiking in a biphasic manner with both the increase and decrease in excitability regulated by glutamate transporters.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the TBOA effects on both excitation and inhibition.

claims.claim: In Golgi cells classified as pausing cells, climbing fiber stimulation decreased the spike frequency from 6.7 ± 0.6 Hz to 3.3 ± 0.5 Hz for 93 ± 16 ms.
claims.source: In GoCs classified as pausing cells, CF stimulation decreased the spike frequency from 6.7 ± 0.6 Hz to 3.3 ± 0.5 Hz (p<10−4, paired t-test) for 93 ± 16 ms (n = 9 of 18 cells), which was equivalent to a reduction of the AP probability from 0.13 ± 0.01 to 0.07 ± 0.01 (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The climbing fiber-evoked average spike frequency was correlated with the climbing fiber-EPSC amplitude across all Golgi cells.
claims.source: Not surprisingly, the CF-evoked average spike frequency (over 40 ms post CF-stimulation) was correlated with the CF-EPSC amplitude across all GoCs (Figure 5E, R2 = 0.2; n = 25, p=0.02).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: There was no correlation between the cumulative ratio and the EPSC amplitude.
claims.source: However, we did not find a correlation between the cumulative ratio and the EPSC amplitude (Figure 5F) nor the cumulative ratio and the CF-evoked average spike frequency (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: There was no correlation between the cumulative ratio and the climbing fiber-evoked average spike frequency.
claims.source: However, we did not find a correlation between the cumulative ratio and the EPSC amplitude (Figure 5F) nor the cumulative ratio and the CF-evoked average spike frequency (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Golgi cell pauses did not result from intrinsic mechanisms that dictate the frequency of firing after depolarization.
claims.source: This suggests that GoC pauses did not result from intrinsic mechanisms that dictate the frequency of firing after depolarization, as occurs with PF- and MF-synaptic stimulation (see below).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between cumulative ratio and spike frequency.

claims.claim: Golgi cells express mGluR2, a Gi/Go coupled glutamate receptor that reduces excitability by activating inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs).
claims.source: Alternatively, GoCs express mGluR2, a Gi/Go coupled glutamate receptor that reduces excitability by activating inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs; Ohishi et al., 1994; Neki et al., 1996; Luján et al., 1997; Nakanishi, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber-spillover could suppress Golgi cell spiking via mGluR2-mediated GIRK activation.
claims.source: CF-spillover could thus suppress GoC spiking via mGluR2-mediated GIRK activation, as occurs following strong or high frequency PF stimulation (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known mGluR2 function and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: TBOA increased the initial climbing fiber-evoked spiking probability in Golgi cells showing climbing fiber-induced pauses.
claims.source: In the subset of GoCs showing CF-induced pauses (Figure 6A), TBOA increased the initial CF-evoked spiking probability (Figure 6B and D) as well as enhanced the duration of the subsequent pause period (from 93.3 ± 16 ms to 183 ± 23 ms; n = 9, p=0.01, paired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: TBOA enhanced the duration of the subsequent pause period following climbing fiber stimulation.
claims.source: In the subset of GoCs showing CF-induced pauses (Figure 6A), TBOA increased the initial CF-evoked spiking probability (Figure 6B and D) as well as enhanced the duration of the subsequent pause period (from 93.3 ± 16 ms to 183 ± 23 ms; n = 9, p=0.01, paired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Inhibition of mGluR2s entirely blocked post-excitation pausing in Golgi cells.
claims.source: Inhibition of mGluR2s entirely blocked post-excitation pausing, returning the GoC spiking to baseline levels (Figure 6C; TBOA + LY341495 = 6.0 ± 0.9 and 6.7 ± 0.5 Hz, respectively; n = 9, p=0.28, paired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: mGluR2 inhibition did not significantly change the number of action potentials added with climbing fiber-stimulation.
claims.source: Furthermore, mGluR2 inhibition did not significantly change the number APs added with CF-stimulation and resulted in a cumulative ratio comparable to that of non-pause GoCs (0.89 ± 0.04 n = 12 and 0.93 ± 0.06; n = 9, p=0.57, unpaired t-test and Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber-induced pausing results from spillover activation of mGluR2s.
claims.source: Thus, CF-induced pausing results from spillover activation of mGluR2s.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the LY341495 blockade of pausing.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber stimulation generates a rapid increase in Golgi cell excitability which can be followed by a longer-lasting suppression of spiking.
claims.source: Together, these results demonstrate that CF stimulation generates a rapid increase in GoC excitability which can be followed by a longer-lasting suppression of spiking.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber-induced inhibition happens in the absence of functional inhibitory connections.
claims.source: CF-induced inhibition happens in the absence of functional inhibitory connections, can be unmasked by uptake inhibition, and is dependent upon postsynaptic mGluR2 activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental design blocking inhibitory receptors.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber-induced inhibition can be unmasked by uptake inhibition.
claims.source: CF-induced inhibition happens in the absence of functional inhibitory connections, can be unmasked by uptake inhibition, and is dependent upon postsynaptic mGluR2 activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the TBOA experiments.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber-induced inhibition is dependent upon postsynaptic mGluR2 activation.
claims.source: CF-induced inhibition happens in the absence of functional inhibitory connections, can be unmasked by uptake inhibition, and is dependent upon postsynaptic mGluR2 activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the LY341495 experiments.

claims.claim: There was a linear relationship between the spiking induced by direct current injection and the subsequent Golgi cell spiking suppression suggestive of intrinsic spike resetting.
claims.source: Indeed, we found a linear relationship between the spiking induced by direct current injection and the subsequent GoC spiking suppression suggestive of intrinsic spike resetting (Solinas et al., 2007b; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Blocking mGluR2 receptors had no effect on pausing following current injection.
claims.source: However, blocking mGluR2 receptors had no effect, whereas blocking mGluR2 receptors selectively abolished the pause following CF stimulation (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Blocking mGluR2 receptors selectively abolished the pause following climbing fiber stimulation.
claims.source: However, blocking mGluR2 receptors had no effect, whereas blocking mGluR2 receptors selectively abolished the pause following CF stimulation (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber-evoked pausing of Golgi cells are not the result of phase resetting mechanisms that regulate pacemaking activity.
claims.source: These results suggest that CF-evoked pausing of GoCs are not the result of phase resetting mechanisms that regulate pacemaking activity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of mGluR2 blockade on CF-evoked vs. current injection-evoked pausing.

claims.claim: Stimulation of either parallel fiber or mossy fiber afferents generated a biphasic pattern of Golgi cell spiking, with the synaptically-evoked action potentials followed by a rapid and brief suppression of spiking.
claims.source: We next sought to determine the effect of single PF or MF stimuli on GoC firing. Stimulation of either afferent generated a biphasic pattern of GoC spiking, with the synaptically-evoked APs followed by a rapid and brief suppression of spiking (Figure 7A and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The pattern of parallel fiber and mossy fiber induced spiking was unaffected either by TBOA or TBOA + LY341495.
claims.source: In contrast to CF stimulation, the pattern of PF and MF induced spiking was unaffected either by TBOA or TBOA + LY341495 (Figure 7A–7D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The insensitivity of parallel fiber and mossy fiber spiking to TBOA is consistent with the insensitivity of the parallel fiber and mossy fiber EPSCs to inhibition of glutamate transport.
claims.source: The insensitivity of spiking to TBOA is consistent with the insensitivity of the PF and MF EPSCs to inhibition of glutamate transport (see Figure 1), and suggests that the pause in spiking reflects a resetting of tonic spike rate (or spike synchronization) due to intrinsic mechanisms that set the interspike interval.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of EPSC and spiking data.

claims.claim: The pause in spiking following parallel fiber and mossy fiber stimulation reflects a resetting of tonic spike rate due to intrinsic mechanisms that set the interspike interval.
claims.source: The insensitivity of spiking to TBOA is consistent with the insensitivity of the PF and MF EPSCs to inhibition of glutamate transport (see Figure 1), and suggests that the pause in spiking reflects a resetting of tonic spike rate (or spike synchronization) due to intrinsic mechanisms that set the interspike interval.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the insensitivity to TBOA and mGluR2 blockade.

claims.claim: The parallel fiber and mossy fiber cumulative ratio was correlated with the spike frequency.
claims.source: Supporting this idea, the PF and MF cumulative ratio was correlated with the spike frequency (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Both spillover and synaptic signaling modes can trigger biphasic modulation of Golgi cell excitability, but the underlying mechanisms mediating these changes are markedly different.
claims.source: These results highlight further differences in spillover and synaptic signaling to GoCs. Whereas both modes of transmission can trigger biphasic modulation of excitability, the underlying mechanisms mediating these changes are markedly different.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential pharmacological sensitivities of CF vs. PF/MF responses.

claims.claim: The heterogeneity of climbing fiber-evoked responses is not a result of receptor expression, since all the tested Golgi cells had a similar response to the exogenous mGluR2 agonist.
claims.source: These data show that the heterogeneity of CF-evoked responses is not a result of receptor expression, since all the tested GoCs had a similar response to the exogenous mGluR2 agonist.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing all tested GoCs responded to DCG-IV.

claims.claim: Golgi cells with a large climbing fiber-evoked LY341495-sensitive current exhibited a robust pause following climbing fiber stimulation.
claims.source: As expected, GoCs with a large CF-evoked LY341495-sensitive current exhibited a robust pause following CF stimulation whereas GoCs with a small or undetectable CF-evoked LY341495-sensitive current did not exhibit pausing behavior (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Golgi cells with a small or undetectable climbing fiber-evoked LY341495-sensitive current did not exhibit pausing behavior.
claims.source: As expected, GoCs with a large CF-evoked LY341495-sensitive current exhibited a robust pause following CF stimulation whereas GoCs with a small or undetectable CF-evoked LY341495-sensitive current did not exhibit pausing behavior (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Across nine Golgi cells there was a correlation between the LY341495-sensitive charge and the cumulative ratio.
claims.source: Across nine GoCs there was a correlation between the LY341495-sensitive charge and the cumulative ratio, further confirming that CF-evoked pausing results from mGluR activation (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: The subcellular location of spillover signaling to Golgi cells, rather than differences in receptor expression give rise to the observed response heterogeneity.
claims.source: Altogether, these results suggest that the subcellular location of spillover signaling to GoCs, rather than differences in receptor expression give rise to the observed response heterogeneity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the uniform mGluR2 expression but variable CF-evoked mGluR2 currents.

claims.claim: Cerebellar climbing fibers signal to Golgi cells by glutamate spillover.
claims.source: Here, we show that cerebellar CFs signal to GoCs by glutamate spillover.
claims.evidence: This is the primary conclusion of the study supported by all experimental data.

claims.claim: Spillover generates direct excitation through activation of AMPARs in Golgi cells.
claims.source: Spillover generates direct excitation through activation of AMPARs, as well as inhibition through activation of mGluRs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing NBQX-sensitive EPSCs.

claims.claim: Spillover generates inhibition through activation of mGluRs in Golgi cells.
claims.source: Spillover generates direct excitation through activation of AMPARs, as well as inhibition through activation of mGluRs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing LY341495-sensitive pausing.

claims.claim: The ability of glutamate spillover to inhibit Golgi cell firing suggests that mGluR-mediated inhibition may contribute to the transient pauses in Golgi cell tonic firing reported in vivo by stimulation of the inferior olive.
claims.source: The ability of glutamate spillover to inhibit GoC firing suggests that mGluR-mediated inhibition may contribute to the transient pauses in GoC tonic firing reported in vivo by stimulation of the inferior olive (Schulman and Bloom, 1981; Xu and Edgley, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings and prior in vivo observations.

claims.claim: Antagonizing the mGluR2 receptor blocks the pause in Golgi cell firing conferred by climbing fiber spillover.
claims.source: We show that antagonizing the mGluR2 receptor blocks the pause in GoC firing conferred by CF spillover, further supporting the importance of mGluR2 inhibition of GoC activity seen in vivo (Holtzman et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data with LY341495.

claims.claim: Climbing fibers were suggested to innervate Golgi cells via thin collateral branches.
claims.source: Whereas CFs were suggested to innervate GoCs via thin collateral branches (Shinoda et al., 2000), recent work failed to find evidence for anatomical synaptic contacts between CFs and GoCs (Galliano et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior anatomical work.

claims.claim: Recent work failed to find evidence for anatomical synaptic contacts between climbing fibers and Golgi cells.
claims.source: Whereas CFs were suggested to innervate GoCs via thin collateral branches (Shinoda et al., 2000), recent work failed to find evidence for anatomical synaptic contacts between CFs and GoCs (Galliano et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to recent anatomical work.

claims.claim: Identification of spillover signaling may reconcile conflicting anatomical and functional results showing a lack of synaptic connections between climbing fibers and Golgi cells yet functional consequences of climbing fiber stimulation.
claims.source: Our identification of spillover signaling may reconcile conflicting anatomical and functional results showing a lack of synaptic connections between CFs and GoCs yet functional consequences of CF stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the current findings in the context of prior conflicting results.

claims.claim: Golgi cells extend short basal dendrites in the granule cell layer to sample mossy fiber activity.
claims.source: GoCs extend short basal dendrites in the granule cell layer to sample MF activity (Marr, 1969; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Ito, 2006; Kanichay and Silver, 2008) and also extend 2–3 apical dendrites into the molecular layer to receive several thousand PF inputs (Vos et al., 1999; Ito, 2006; Robberechts et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Golgi cells extend 2–3 apical dendrites into the molecular layer to receive several thousand parallel fiber inputs.
claims.source: GoCs extend short basal dendrites in the granule cell layer to sample MF activity (Marr, 1969; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Ito, 2006; Kanichay and Silver, 2008) and also extend 2–3 apical dendrites into the molecular layer to receive several thousand PF inputs (Vos et al., 1999; Ito, 2006; Robberechts et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber spillover signaling is expected to occur on apical Golgi cell dendrites in the molecular layer, due to their proximity to climbing fibers that innervate Purkinje cell dendrites.
claims.source: We expect that CF spillover signaling occurs on apical GoC dendrites in the ML, due to their proximity to CFs that innervate PC dendrites.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical arrangement of CFs and GoC dendrites.

claims.claim: Spillover signaling may enable integration of synaptic inputs in apical dendrites over a broader time window in contrast to the narrow window of integration of synaptic inputs arising in basal dendrites.
claims.source: Spillover signaling may enable integration of synaptic inputs in apical dendrites over a broader time window in contrast to the narrow window of integration of synaptic inputs arising in basal dendrites.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the slow kinetics of spillover transmission.

claims.claim: Single mossy fiber boutons are contacted by ~50–100 granule cell dendrites and usually a single Golgi cell axon.
claims.source: Here, single mossy fiber boutons are contacted by ~50–100 GC dendrites and usually a single GoC axon (Crowley et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The influence of Golgi cells is facilitated by the complex glomerular geometry that enables GABA released from Golgi cells to spillover to adjacent, non-synaptically coupled granule cells.
claims.source: The influence of GoCs is facilitated by the complex glomerular geometry that enables GABA released from GoCs to spillover to adjacent, non-synaptically coupled GCs (Hamann et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on GABA spillover.

claims.claim: The extensive ramification of the complex Golgi cell axon allows a single Golgi cell to contact many glomeruli.
claims.source: The extensive ramification of the complex GoC axon also allows a single GoC to contact many glomeruli (Ito, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Synaptic activation of Golgi cells generates feedforward phasic inhibition of granule cells.
claims.source: Synaptic activation of GoCs generates feedforward phasic inhibition of GCs, and pacemaker activity contributes to tonic inhibition of GCs (Brickley et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Pacemaker activity of Golgi cells contributes to tonic inhibition of granule cells.
claims.source: Synaptic activation of GoCs generates feedforward phasic inhibition of GCs, and pacemaker activity contributes to tonic inhibition of GCs (Brickley et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber-excitation of Golgi cells has the potential to influence the excitability of thousands of granule cells.
claims.source: Thus CF-excitation of GoCs has the potential to influence the excitability of thousands of GCs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the extensive connectivity of GoCs with GCs.

claims.claim: Golgi cells receive GABAergic inhibition from Lugaro cells at a ratio of 10:1 Lugaro cell:Golgi cell.
claims.source: In addition to their glutamatergic inputs, GoCs receive GABAergic inhibition from Lugaro cells (at a ratio of 10:1 LC:GoC; Dieudonné and Dumoulin, 2000; Dumoulin et al., 2001), cerebellar nuclear cells (Ankri et al., 2015), and other GoCs but not MLIs (Dugué et al., 2009; Hull and Regehr, 2012; Szoboszlay et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Golgi cells receive GABAergic inhibition from cerebellar nuclear cells.
claims.source: In addition to their glutamatergic inputs, GoCs receive GABAergic inhibition from Lugaro cells (at a ratio of 10:1 LC:GoC; Dieudonné and Dumoulin, 2000; Dumoulin et al., 2001), cerebellar nuclear cells (Ankri et al., 2015), and other GoCs but not MLIs (Dugué et al., 2009; Hull and Regehr, 2012; Szoboszlay et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Golgi cells receive GABAergic inhibition from other Golgi cells but not molecular layer interneurons.
claims.source: In addition to their glutamatergic inputs, GoCs receive GABAergic inhibition from Lugaro cells (at a ratio of 10:1 LC:GoC; Dieudonné and Dumoulin, 2000; Dumoulin et al., 2001), cerebellar nuclear cells (Ankri et al., 2015), and other GoCs but not MLIs (Dugué et al., 2009; Hull and Regehr, 2012; Szoboszlay et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Reciprocal connections between granule cells and Golgi cells creates a traditional feedback inhibitory loop.
claims.source: Reciprocal connections between GCs and GoCs thus creates a traditional feedback inhibitory loop, that together with feedforward and tonic inhibition, maintain sparse population activity in the GC layer (D'Angelo et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Feedforward, feedback, and tonic inhibition maintain sparse population activity in the granule cell layer.
claims.source: Reciprocal connections between GCs and GoCs thus creates a traditional feedback inhibitory loop, that together with feedforward and tonic inhibition, maintain sparse population activity in the GC layer (D'Angelo et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Reciprocal GABAergic synapses between Golgi cells or connections from Lugaro cells or recurrent Purkinje cell-Golgi cell connections could contribute to climbing fiber-evoked pausing in vivo.
claims.source: We speculate that reciprocal GABAergic synapses between GoCs or connections from Lugaro cells or recurrent PC-GoC connections (Witter et al., 2016) could contribute to CF-evoked pausing in vivo, a possibility that we did not test due to the difficulty of identifying CF-evoked EPSCs in the presence of intact inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms in vivo.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber-mediated regulation of Golgi cell spiking displayed distinct temporal properties compared to synaptic signaling from parallel fibers and mossy fibers.
claims.source: We found that CF-mediated regulation of GoC spiking displayed distinct temporal properties compared to synaptic signaling from PF and MFs.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claims.claim: Single parallel fiber and mossy fiber stimuli triggered rapid Golgi cell spiking followed by a short-latency pause in tonic firing that was unaffected by mGluR2 antagonism.
claims.source: Single PF and MF stimuli triggered rapid GoC spiking followed by a short-latency pause in tonic firing that was unaffected by mGluR2 antagonism.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The brief pause after parallel fiber and mossy fiber stimulation is likely due to the intrinsic pacemaker firing of Golgi cells that is synchronized across trials.
claims.source: It is likely that this brief pause is due to the intrinsic pacemaker firing of GoCs that is synchronized across trials (Vos et al., 1999; D'Angelo, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the insensitivity to mGluR2 blockade and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Golgi cells respond to afferent stimulation with a short burst of spikes that disrupts their intrinsic pacemaker activity.
claims.source: GoCs respond to afferent stimulation with a short burst of spikes that disrupts their intrinsic pacemaker activity (Solinas et al., 2007b, 2007a).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The pause seen after synaptic stimulation or current injection results from the synchronized reset in the pacemaker activity of the Golgi cell.
claims.source: As a result, the pause seen after synaptic stimulation or current injection results from the synchronized reset in the pacemaker activity of the GoC.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the intrinsic properties of GoCs and experimental data.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber evoked suppression of Golgi cell spiking depended on mGluR activation rather than intrinsic spike resetting.
claims.source: In contrast, CF evoked suppression of GoC spiking depended on mGluR activation rather than intrinsic spike resetting.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing LY341495 sensitivity.

claims.claim: Both climbing fiber excitation and inhibition were enhanced by application of the glutamate transporter antagonist TBOA.
claims.source: Both CF excitation and inhibition were enhanced by application of the glutamate transporter antagonist TBOA, but suppression of CF spiking was selectively blocked by mGluR2 antagonism, suggesting suppression results from mGluR-induced inhibition, similar to PF burst stimulation that activates postsynaptic mGluR2 on GoCs (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003; Nakanishi, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data with TBOA.

claims.claim: Suppression of climbing fiber spiking was selectively blocked by mGluR2 antagonism.
claims.source: Both CF excitation and inhibition were enhanced by application of the glutamate transporter antagonist TBOA, but suppression of CF spiking was selectively blocked by mGluR2 antagonism, suggesting suppression results from mGluR-induced inhibition, similar to PF burst stimulation that activates postsynaptic mGluR2 on GoCs (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003; Nakanishi, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data with LY341495.

claims.claim: Suppression of climbing fiber-evoked Golgi cell spiking results from mGluR-induced inhibition, similar to parallel fiber burst stimulation that activates postsynaptic mGluR2 on Golgi cells.
claims.source: Both CF excitation and inhibition were enhanced by application of the glutamate transporter antagonist TBOA, but suppression of CF spiking was selectively blocked by mGluR2 antagonism, suggesting suppression results from mGluR-induced inhibition, similar to PF burst stimulation that activates postsynaptic mGluR2 on GoCs (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003; Nakanishi, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological data and supported by citations.

claims.claim: In the intact brain, multiple active climbing fibers may provide spillover to Golgi cells to produce a response under physiological conditions.
claims.source: In the intact brain, multiple active CFs may provide spillover to GoCs to produce a response under physiological conditions.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about physiological conditions based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Spillover dependent mGluR-mediated inhibition may augment feedforward GABAergic synaptic inhibition imposed by other Golgi cells and Lugaro cells.
claims.source: In addition, spillover dependent mGluR-mediated inhibition may augment feedforward GABAergic synaptic inhibition imposed by other GoCs and Lugaro cells, although these possibilities remain to be tested.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential interactions with other inhibitory mechanisms.

claims.claim: mGluR2 is randomly distributed across the entire somatodendritic domain and axon of Golgi cells.
claims.source: Unlike mGluR1/5 subunits that preferentially localize near excitatory synapses, mGluR2 is randomly distributed across the entire somatodendritic domain and axon of GoCs (Luján et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The preferential activation of mGluR2 by single climbing fiber stimuli likely reflects the accessibility of spillover glutamate to reach sufficiently large regions of extrasynaptic Golgi cell membranes to recruit detectable mGluR2-mediated GIRK activation.
claims.source: The preferential activation of mGluR2 by single CF stimuli likely reflects the accessibility of spillover glutamate to reach sufficiently large regions of extrasynaptic GoC membranes to recruit detectable mGluR2-mediated GIRK activation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of mGluR2 and the nature of spillover transmission.

claims.claim: Spillover actions are largely regulated by glutamate clearance in the extracellular space and the proximity of postsynaptic receptors to the release sites.
claims.source: Because spillover is not confined to an anatomical post-synaptic site, its actions are largely regulated by glutamate clearance in the extracellular space and the proximity of postsynaptic receptors to the release sites.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about spillover transmission.

claims.claim: Transport blockade enhances the duration of the mGluR2-mediated pause.
claims.source: Our results showing that transport blockade enhances the duration of the mGluR2-mediated pause are consistent with this idea.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data with TBOA.

claims.claim: Glutamate release at parallel fiber and mossy fiber synapses is likely constrained to peri-synaptic regions by a high density of glutamate transporters at excitatory synapses.
claims.source: In contrast, glutamate release at PF and MF synapses is likely constrained to peri-synaptic regions by a high density of glutamate transporters at excitatory synapses, such that extrasynaptic mGluR2 activation is controlled by the strength and duration of synaptic stimulation (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the insensitivity of PF/MF EPSCs to TBOA and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Extrasynaptic mGluR2 activation at parallel fiber and mossy fiber synapses is controlled by the strength and duration of synaptic stimulation.
claims.source: In contrast, glutamate release at PF and MF synapses is likely constrained to peri-synaptic regions by a high density of glutamate transporters at excitatory synapses, such that extrasynaptic mGluR2 activation is controlled by the strength and duration of synaptic stimulation (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Glutamate released by single parallel fiber and mossy fiber stimuli was insufficient to activate mGluR2-mediated inhibition, even when glutamate transporters are blocked.
claims.source: Our results confirm that glutamate released by single PF and MF stimuli was insufficient to activate mGluR2-mediated inhibition, even when glutamate transporters are blocked.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no effect of LY341495 on PF/MF-evoked pausing.

claims.claim: Golgi cells in vivo do not show excitation but exclusively show a pause in firing in response to climbing fiber stimulation.
claims.source: Golgi cells in vivo do not show excitation but exclusively show a pause in firing in response to climbing fiber stimulation (Xu and Edgley, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to in vivo studies.

claims.claim: Differences in experimental approaches between in vivo and in vitro studies may contribute to the discrepancy in outcomes regarding Golgi cell responses to climbing fiber stimulation.
claims.source: It is possible that differences in experimental approaches between in vivo and in vitro studies contribute to this discrepancy in outcomes.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the source of discrepancies.

claims.claim: The discrepancy between in vivo and in vitro results reflects the difference in the probability of identifying a 'paired' recording between a particular climbing fiber and Golgi cell in the two preparations.
claims.source: We speculate that the discrepancy between in vivo and in vitro results reflects the difference in the probability of identifying a 'paired' recording between a particular CF and GoC in the two preparations.

claims.claim: Climbing fibers can generate a range of Golgi cell responses including excitation only, biphasic excitation-inhibition and inhibition only, depending on the complement of glutamate receptors responding to spillover.
claims.source: We expect that CFs can generate a range of GoC responses including excitation only, biphasic excitation-inhibition and inhibition only, depending on the complement of glutamate receptors responding to spillover.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: mGluRs have a higher affinity for glutamate than AMPARs.
claims.source: Since mGluRs have a higher affinity for glutamate than AMPARs (Malherbe et al., 2001; Traynelis et al., 2010), it is possible that most GoCs in vivo exhibit solely an inhibitory response, but due to our selection criteria for confirming the CF source of glutamate, all of our GoC recordings have AMPA receptor components that will undoubtedly cause excitation.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Most Golgi cells in vivo may exhibit solely an inhibitory response to climbing fiber stimulation.
claims.source: Since mGluRs have a higher affinity for glutamate than AMPARs (Malherbe et al., 2001; Traynelis et al., 2010), it is possible that most GoCs in vivo exhibit solely an inhibitory response, but due to our selection criteria for confirming the CF source of glutamate, all of our GoC recordings have AMPA receptor components that will undoubtedly cause excitation.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on receptor affinities and experimental selection criteria.

claims.claim: Golgi cells are responsible for regulating the responsiveness of granule cells to mossy fiber afferent activity and thus setting the tone of information flow through the cerebellar cortex.
claims.source: GoCs are responsible for regulating the responsiveness of GCs to MF afferent activity and thus setting the tone of information flow through the cerebellar cortex.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about GoC function.

claims.claim: The activity of Golgi cells sets the firing threshold as well as controls the timing of granule cell firing and subsequent information transfer to Purkinje cells.
claims.source: The activity of GoCs sets the firing threshold as well as controls the timing of GC firing and subsequent information transfer to Purkinje cells (Gabbiani et al., 1994; De Schutter et al., 2000; Vos et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Tonic and spillover inhibition from Golgi cells play a large role in determining the number of granule cells able to respond to a given mossy fiber input.
claims.source: Tonic and spillover inhibition from GoCs play a large role in determining the number of GCs able to respond to a given MF input (Brickley et al., 1996; Rossi et al., 2003; Duguid et al., 2012), which in turn helps generate a sparse representation that is thought to enhance the storage capacity of the cerebellum.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Sparse representation generated by Golgi cell inhibition is thought to enhance the storage capacity of the cerebellum.
claims.source: Tonic and spillover inhibition from GoCs play a large role in determining the number of GCs able to respond to a given MF input (Brickley et al., 1996; Rossi et al., 2003; Duguid et al., 2012), which in turn helps generate a sparse representation that is thought to enhance the storage capacity of the cerebellum.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Phasic inhibition generated by parallel fiber and mossy fiber activity serves to synchronize inhibition, and by extension granule cell activity generating center-surround inhibition.
claims.source: Phasic inhibition generated by PF and MF activity serves to synchronize inhibition, and by extension GC activity generating center-surround inhibition (Vos et al., 1999; D'Angelo and De Zeeuw, 2009; Vervaeke et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber input could serve to demarcate groups of Golgi cells depending on the type of response to climbing fiber input to promote spatial filtering of mossy fiber signals.
claims.source: Since GoCs regulate transmission at the mossy fiber-granule cell relay, CF input could serve to demarcate groups of GoCs depending on the type of response to CF input (with or without an mGluR-induced pause) to promote spatial filtering of mossy fiber signals (Mitchell and Silver, 2000a, 2000b, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the heterogeneous GoC responses and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Recent models emphasize the role of the granule cell layer in the timing of motor commands.
claims.source: In addition, recent models have moved away from the granule cell layer being a simple spatial filter to emphasize its role in the timing of motor commands (Yamazaki and Tanaka, 2009; Rössert et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent modeling work.

claims.claim: Golgi cells set the time window for granule cell spiking and time is encoded through the sequential activation of populations of granule cells.
claims.source: In this context, GoCs set the time window for GC spiking and time is encoded through the sequential activation of populations of GCs.
claims.evidence: This is based on recent models of cerebellar function.

claims.claim: Disrupting the cerebellar cortical circuit leads to changes in learned response times while failing to abolish the learned response itself.
claims.source: Indeed, results from behavioral assays in combination with lesioning studies have shown that disrupting the cerebellar cortical circuit leads to changes in learned response times while failing to abolish the learned response itself (Perrett et al., 1993; Raymond et al., 1996; Prestori et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claims.claim: Spillover may serve to desynchronize cells within each layer of the cortex to promote efficient learning.
claims.source: In the context of timing, spillover may serve to desynchronize cells within each layer of the cortex to promote efficient learning.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of spillover.

claims.claim: Heterogeneity can arise from differential connectivity patterns between granule cells and mossy fibers, as well as by recurrent inhibition from the Golgi cell network which enhances sparse granule cell activity.
claims.source: Heterogeneity can arise from differential connectivity patterns between GCs and mossy fibers, as well as by recurrent inhibition from the GoC network which enhances sparse GC activity.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about sources of heterogeneity.

claims.source: Thus, heterogeneity in CF-mediated mGluR activation on GoCs could provide as a source of variability in GCL activity.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and modeling work.

claims.source: Here, conjunctive stimulation of CFs and peripheral inputs may lead to LTD at the MF-GC relay and/or plasticity at excitatory GoC synapses (Xu and Edgley, 2008; Robberechts et al., 2010).

results.result: Climbing fiber stimulation evokes EPSCs in Golgi cells with distinct characteristics from parallel fiber and mossy fiber EPSCs. CF-evoked EPSCs show all-or-none behavior, slow kinetics, strong paired-pulse depression, and high sensitivity to the glutamate transporter blocker TBOA, establishing criteria for identifying spillover-mediated transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C40 and C43 provide comprehensive experimental characterization of CF-evoked EPSCs using electrical stimulation, pharmacology (NBQX, TBOA), and comparison with PF and MF inputs. The data in Figure 1 demonstrate distinct kinetic and pharmacological properties consistent with spillover transmission, with appropriate statistical comparisons and controls.

results.result: NMDA receptors can sense glutamate spillover from climbing fibers under depolarizing conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by experimental data showing CPP-sensitive currents at +40 mV following single CF stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). However, the functional significance under physiological conditions remains speculative as acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of climbing fibers in CRH-ChR2 mice evokes spillover EPSCs in Golgi cells similar to electrical stimulation, and Golgi cells can sense spillover from multiple climbing fibers.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 and C52-C55 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing that light-evoked EPSCs have similar characteristics to electrically-evoked EPSCs (all-or-none, strong PPD, slow kinetics). The step-wise increases in amplitude with increasing light intensity provide evidence for multiple CF recruitment.

results.result: Increasing extracellular calcium from 2.0 to 2.5 mM increases CF-GoC EPSC amplitude and prolongs decay without altering TBOA sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing calcium-dependent changes in EPSC properties consistent with increased release probability. The lack of change in TBOA sensitivity suggests transporter regulation is not altered by this modest increase in spillover.

results.result: All three afferent pathways (PF, MF, CF) can recruit Golgi cell spiking but with distinct temporal profiles. CF stimulation produces a modest increase in peak spike probability within a broader window compared to the rapid, narrow windows of PF and MF stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C61 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing peristimulus histograms with appropriate statistical comparisons. The data demonstrate that despite different temporal dynamics, all three pathways add similar numbers of action potentials over 40 ms.

results.result: TBOA reveals biphasic regulation of Golgi cell spiking by climbing fiber stimulation, with both excitation and subsequent inhibition enhanced by blocking glutamate transporters.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4B showing TBOA increases peak spiking probability over 250% and subsequently reduces AP probability to ~70% of baseline. This demonstrates transporter-dependent regulation of both phases of the response.

results.result: Golgi cells show heterogeneous responses to CF stimulation, with some cells exhibiting pausing behavior. The CF-evoked spike frequency correlates with EPSC amplitude, but the cumulative ratio (pausing) does not correlate with EPSC amplitude or spike frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing classification of pause vs. non-pause cells and correlation analyses. The lack of correlation between cumulative ratio and EPSC amplitude/spike frequency suggests pausing is not simply due to intrinsic mechanisms related to depolarization magnitude.

results.result: CF-induced pausing of Golgi cells results from spillover activation of mGluR2 receptors. TBOA enhances both the initial excitation and the subsequent pause, while the mGluR2 antagonist LY341495 completely blocks the pause without affecting the number of added action potentials.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C81 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing pharmacological dissection with TBOA and LY341495. The selective blockade of pausing by LY341495 while preserving excitation provides compelling evidence for mGluR2-mediated inhibition independent of GABAergic mechanisms.

results.result: CF-evoked pausing is mechanistically distinct from intrinsic spike resetting. While current injection produces pausing that is insensitive to mGluR2 blockade, CF-evoked pausing is selectively abolished by LY341495.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing differential effects of LY341495 on current injection-evoked vs. CF-evoked pausing. This demonstrates that CF pausing is not simply due to phase resetting of pacemaker activity.

results.result: PF and MF stimulation produce biphasic spiking patterns that are insensitive to TBOA and LY341495, suggesting the pause reflects intrinsic spike resetting rather than mGluR2 activation. This contrasts with CF-mediated regulation which depends on mGluR2.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 are supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing that PF/MF-evoked pausing is unaffected by TBOA or LY341495, and the cumulative ratio correlates with spike frequency (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). This establishes mechanistic differences between spillover and synaptic signaling modes.

results.result: The heterogeneity of CF-evoked responses is not due to differential mGluR2 expression, as all tested Golgi cells respond similarly to the exogenous mGluR2 agonist DCG-IV. Instead, the magnitude of CF-evoked mGluR2 activation correlates with pausing behavior, suggesting subcellular location of spillover signaling determines response heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 are supported by experimental data in Figures 8 and 9 showing uniform responses to DCG-IV across pause and non-pause cells, but correlation between LY341495-sensitive charge and cumulative ratio. This suggests spatial factors rather than receptor expression determine response variability.

results.result: Golgi cells are the principal inhibitory neurons at the input stage of the cerebellum, providing feedforward and feedback inhibition through mossy fiber and parallel fiber synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C23 represent established knowledge about Golgi cell function in cerebellar circuitry, supported by the literature and providing necessary context for the study.

results.result: Prior work shows that Golgi cell activity is regulated by CF stimulation in vivo, yet there is conflicting evidence regarding anatomical synaptic connections between CFs and Golgi cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C24-C26 accurately summarize prior literature showing functional CF-GoC interactions in vivo but lack of anatomical evidence for direct synapses. This establishes the motivation for the current study.

results.result: The study demonstrates that climbing fibers signal to Golgi cells through glutamate spillover, activating both ionotropic (AMPAR) and metabotropic (mGluR2) receptors to provide flexible control over Golgi cell excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8, C27-C28, and C97-C99 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence from voltage-clamp, current-clamp, and pharmacological experiments presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The identification of spillover signaling reconciles conflicting anatomical and functional results and may explain in vivo observations of CF-induced pausing of Golgi cell firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C100, C101, and C104 represent reasonable interpretations of the data in the context of prior literature. The mGluR2 antagonist experiments provide direct support for the mechanism underlying in vivo pausing observations.

results.result: Golgi cells receive synaptic inputs from parallel fibers on apical dendrites in the molecular layer and from mossy fibers on basal dendrites in the granule cell layer. CF spillover signaling is expected to occur on apical dendrites due to their proximity to CFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 and C105-C107 represent established anatomical knowledge supported by citations. The inference about CF spillover location (C107) is reasonable based on known anatomy, though not directly tested in this study.

results.result: Spillover signaling may enable integration of synaptic inputs in apical dendrites over a broader time window compared to synaptic inputs in basal dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is speculation based on the slow kinetics of spillover transmission. While plausible, this hypothesis about dendritic integration is not directly tested and would require additional experiments examining dendritic processing.

results.result: Golgi cells exert widespread influence on granule cell excitability through multiple mechanisms including feedforward, feedback, and tonic inhibition, with GABA spillover facilitating inhibition of non-synaptically coupled granule cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C119 represent established knowledge about Golgi cell connectivity and function, supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context for understanding the potential impact of CF-mediated GoC regulation.

results.result: In vivo, multiple mechanisms including reciprocal GABAergic connections, Lugaro cell inputs, or multiple active CFs may contribute to CF-evoked pausing and augment mGluR-mediated inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C120, C130, and C131 represent reasonable speculation about in vivo conditions, but these possibilities are explicitly acknowledged as untested by the authors. Additional experiments would be needed to evaluate these hypotheses.

results.result: CF-mediated regulation of Golgi cell spiking displays distinct temporal properties and mechanisms compared to PF and MF synaptic signaling. CF suppression depends on mGluR activation, while PF/MF pausing results from intrinsic pacemaker resetting.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C129 are supported by experimental data comparing the three pathways and their pharmacological sensitivities. The mechanistic distinction is well-established through the differential effects of TBOA and LY341495.

results.result: mGluR2 is randomly distributed across Golgi cell membranes, making it well-positioned to sense spillover glutamate. The preferential activation by CF stimulation reflects the accessibility of spillover glutamate to extrasynaptic receptors, while PF/MF glutamate is constrained by high-density transporters.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C138 integrate established anatomical knowledge (C132) with experimental observations and reasonable inferences about the spatial regulation of glutamate. The differential TBOA sensitivity of CF vs. PF/MF responses supports this interpretation.

results.result: The discrepancy between in vivo observations (exclusively inhibitory responses) and in vitro findings (mixed excitatory and inhibitory responses) may reflect methodological differences in the probability of identifying paired CF-GoC recordings and the higher affinity of mGluRs for glutamate compared to AMPARs.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C144 represent speculation about the source of in vivo/in vitro discrepancies. While the reasoning is plausible and based on known receptor properties (C143), these hypotheses are not directly tested and would require additional experiments to validate.

results.result: Golgi cells regulate granule cell responsiveness, firing threshold, and timing, with tonic and spillover inhibition determining the number of granule cells responding to mossy fiber input and generating sparse representations that enhance cerebellar storage capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149 represent established knowledge about Golgi cell function supported by appropriate citations. These provide important functional context for interpreting the significance of CF-mediated GoC regulation.

results.result: CF input could demarcate groups of Golgi cells to promote spatial filtering of mossy fiber signals, and spillover may serve to desynchronize cells to promote efficient learning in the context of timing-based models of cerebellar function.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C154 represent speculation about functional implications based on recent computational models and behavioral studies. While plausible and grounded in cited literature, these hypotheses about circuit-level function are not directly tested.

results.result: Heterogeneity in CF-mediated mGluR activation on Golgi cells could provide a source of variability in granule cell layer activity, potentially increasing the dynamic range of responses while preventing erratic circuit states.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C157 integrate the experimental findings with computational modeling predictions (C156). While the connection is reasonable, the functional consequences of GoC response heterogeneity on GCL dynamics are speculative and would require additional modeling or experimental work to validate.

results.result: CF spillover may enable local interneuron circuits to monitor PC input and regulate circuit excitation/inhibition, potentially relaying privileged error signal information to the input stage and enhancing response complexity through non-synaptic transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C161 represent speculation about the broader functional implications of CF spillover in cerebellar learning and motor control. While these ideas are conceptually interesting and grounded in the error signal hypothesis, they are not directly tested and represent future directions.

results.result: Background on volume transmission and glutamate spillover establishes that functional connectivity is not strictly synonymous with anatomical connectivity, with extensive prior work demonstrating CF spillover to molecular layer interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C22 accurately summarize established knowledge about volume transmission, glutamate spillover, and prior work on CF-MLI spillover transmission. These provide essential background and motivation for the current study.

results.result: Golgi cells express mGluR2 receptors coupled to GIRK channels that reduce excitability, providing a potential mechanism for CF-spillover to suppress Golgi cell spiking.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 represent established knowledge (C71) and a reasonable hypothesis (C72) that is subsequently tested and confirmed by the experimental data with LY341495.
